newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany urged, Don't force Bosnia refugees home.
newsitem.headline: Germany urged, Don't force Bosnia refugees home.

text.p: Germany's opposition Greens, humanitarian and church groups joined in a last-ditch appeal to regional leaders on Tuesday to drop "dangerous" plans to force 320,000 Bosnian refugees to go home from October 1.
Victims of Bosnia's 43-month ethnic war would become victims again, they said in an open letter to German interior ministers, meeting in Bonn on Thursday to set a repatriation timetable.

They urged against sending refugees home quickly just to save money. The call echoed a plea by the United Nations refugee agency to countries of asylum to delay forcing Bosnian refugees back home. The agency said in Geneva that Bosnia's weekend election showed the difficulty of people returning to ethnic minority areas.

Conservatives in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition blasted the groups' call, saying Germany could not afford to keep the refugees any longer but Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel promised they would not be driven out "heartlessly".

The letter said: "The victims of war and ethnic cleansing will just become victims once again -- this time of a conflict between Germany's federal, regional and local councils which is purely a matter of financial and domestic policy."

The letter, addressed to regional leaders, members of the national parliament and cabinet ministers, said it was still too dangerous to send them to regions dominated by other ethnic groups and urged them to wait until it was safer.

"Bosnian civil war refugees must start going home now," said Wolfgang Zeitlmann, a deputy from the CSU, the Bavarian sister party of Kohl's Christian Democrats, echoing a hardline stance taken recently by development minister Carl-Dieter Spranger.

Germany, which has taken in more Bosnian refugees than the rest of European Union states put together, plans to start forced repatriations in October as a last resort -- if refugees refuse to go home voluntarily.

German regional states, which accommodate and maintain the refugees, and the federal government have given assurances they will only press ahead with their step-by-step repatriation programme once they decide the region is safe enough.

Kerstin Mueller, the Greens' spokeswoman in parliament, said Germany should follow the example of other countries that have taken in refugees, such as Sweden, and heed the advice of refugee agencies by holding back until next spring or summer.

The United Nations' High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) says some 60 percent of Bosnian refugees in Germany are Moslems from areas ethnically cleansed by Bosnian Serbs and it would be too dangerous now for them to return home.

"For many, a return would mean just moving into refugee camps for the winter," Mueller told a news conference, adding that refugees may never be able to return to their homes again and that alternatives had yet to be discussed.
She said Germany should contribute to a reconstruction fund to faciliate their return to their devastated home country.

Kinkel said he also favoured a fund to support refugees' return but commented not all the refugees came from ethnically cleansed areas. He told MDR radio the UNHCR had established 19 safe areas where refugees could start returning.
"There will be no heartless repatriation," he said.
